plants.name: Protea cynaroides
plants.description: A dramatic shrub crowned with dinner-plate-sized flower heads. Rows of silky, pointed pink bracts surround a central cushion of pale, fuzzy florets, like a fiery artichoke in full regalia. It blooms in the middle of the Southern Hemisphere winter, when little else is in flower.
plants.bloomingSeason: April to October, so it is in flower in late July, the middle of the southern winter
plants.location: Fynbos shrublands and mountain slopes of the Western and Eastern Cape, South Africa
plants.funFact: The King Protea is South Africa's national flower. It belongs to a very ancient plant family that dates back to the supercontinent Gondwana, and it has evolved to survive regular wildfires.

plants.name: Echinacea purpurea
plants.description: A sturdy prairie wildflower with daisy-like blooms. Rosy-purple petals droop gracefully around a spiky, copper-orange central cone. In midsummer meadows and cottage gardens it hums with bees and butterflies, and goldfinches visit later to feed on the seed heads.
plants.bloomingSeason: June to August, so it is at its midsummer peak around July 21
plants.location: Native to the prairies and open woodlands of the eastern and central United States, and widely grown in gardens across North America and Europe
plants.funFact: The 'cone' in the center is made up of hundreds of tiny, spiny florets, and its name comes from the Greek word 'echinos', meaning hedgehog. Indigenous peoples of the Great Plains used the plant medicinally for generations.

plants.name: Lavandula angustifolia
plants.description: A silvery, aromatic shrub whose slender spikes of tiny violet-blue flowers ripple across sunny hillsides and fields in long, perfumed rows. The scent hangs warm in the summer air and draws crowds of bees.
plants.bloomingSeason: Early to mid-summer, so it is in bloom or near peak in July in the Northern Hemisphere
plants.location: Sunny Mediterranean hillsides and cultivated fields in southern Europe, such as Provence in France, and temperate gardens across the Northern Hemisphere
plants.funFact: The name lavender is often linked to the Latin 'lavare', meaning 'to wash'. Romans used the flowers to scent their baths, and the oil is still a staple of perfumery.
